name: Ignaciano
confidence_why: Ott & Ott (1959, 1967, 1983) and Carvalho & Rose (2018, drawing on Olza Zubiri et al. 2002) all put Ignaciano accent on the second syllable of longer words and the first syllable of disyllables, and the only tension is whether the few initial-accented longer words (sarare 'animal', máyusi 'pineapple') and the surface-initial accents produced by prefix-vowel elision make the system 'phonemic', as the Otts' phoneme sketch says, or a default rule with marked exceptions, as the Otts' own 1983 note and Carvalho & Rose treat it, so the placement is secure but the 'exceptionless' label is too strong.
catalog_quote: Por lo general, el acento prosódico recae en la primera sílaba de palabras bisilábicas y en la segunda de palabras polisilábicas. De otro modo, se indica el acento ortográfico. Ej.: vite "murciélago" / nuyana "voy" / nívape "mi pie" / tijahúchava "repentinamente"
sweep_summary: Only one title-works with stress in the title: Ott, Rebecca B. 1957, 'Datos sobre el acento ignaciano' (Riberalta: ILV) — squarely about Ignaciano word accent, but an unpublished SIL-Bolivia in-house typescript. Its existence is confirmed only bibliographically (Glottolog 113207 via Fabre's Diccionario etnolingüístico, Arawak vol. p. 72, both; no copy, abstract, library holding or later citation was found (archive.org, Google Books, Crossref, Semantic Scholar empty; SIL archive an automated-access block-403, HathiTrust 403, WorldCat 429, scholar.archive. for the session was already exhausted). Priority medium: it is the earliest stress-specific note, but the same authors' 1959 phoneme sketch (held, same 1956-57 field period) almost certainly publishes its content, and Carvalho & Rose 2018 (held) give the fuller analysis. Best statement actually read: Ott & Ott 1959 p. 9 sec. 1. 21, supersedes the 1983 dictionary orthographic note and contradicts counts as exceptionless (the strict set) while confirming the dominant rule (fixed-dominant, as already concluded). Still worth acquiring for this language (outside this search of works with stress in the title's items): Olza Zubiri et al. 2002/2004 grammar (stress pp. 7, 11, 22-23, 36 per Carvalho & Rose) and Jordá 2014 (Lenguas de Bolivia III), both print-only.

new_statements.quote: El acento en ignaciano es fonémico. Ejemplos son: /máyusi/ 'piña', /mayúsi/ 'él tiró (hombre hablando)'; /númama/ 'mi piel', /numáma/ 'mi mandíbula, quijada'. Aunque no se puede predecir en muchas palabras, parece que el tipo más notorio del acento primario, recae en la segunda sílaba de la palabra.
new_statements.translation: Accent in Ignaciano is phonemic. Examples are: /máyusi/ 'pineapple', /mayúsi/ 'he threw (man speaking)'; /númama/ 'my skin', /numáma/ 'my jaw'. Although it cannot be predicted in many words, it seems that the most conspicuous type of primary accent falls on the second syllable of the word.

new_statements.reading: First-hand phonological statement by the same SIL fieldworkers whose 1983 dictionary note is the catalog's deciding source, from the 1956-57 field period that also produced the un-located 1957 'Datos sobre el acento ignaciano'. It calls accent phonemic with minimal pairs and only a dominant (not exceptionless) second-syllable pattern. Read together with Carvalho & Rose 2018 (held; LIAMES 18(1), p. 21: accent 'is best described as falling on the second underlying syllable of the word.., except on bisyllabic words and some rare trisyllabic nouns where it falls on the word-initial syllable'), it contradicts the catalog's 'fixed-strict' (counts as exceptionless (the strict set)) coding while confirming the rule string (second syllable; initial in disyllables): the right bin is fixed-dominant with a lexical initial-accent class plus a systematic surface-initial class from prefix-vowel elision. This matches the reclassify already recorded in for igna1246

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule string (second syllable) and the same qualification already recorded from the 1959 Spanish version (phonemic; unpredictable in many words; second syllable is the most frequent pattern), so it confirms the already-recorded reclassification from strict fixed: second syllable to dominant second with lexical exceptions rather than adding a new contradiction. It adds one genuinely new detail: secondary stress most frequently on the penult. Caveat on custody: the article itself could not be opened (WALS refdb record has no text; De Gruyter blocked twice); the sentence is a verbatim page-cited quotation of the article made by the Stanford Phonology Archive compil…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is contrastive (phonemic) and cannot be predicted in many words, but the dominant pattern is primary stress on the second syllable of the word, with a secondary stress usually on the penultimate syllable. The wording is a statistical dominance claim ('most frequently'), not an exceptionless rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'secondary stress most frequently falls on the penult' (p. 58); this detail is absent from the 1959 Spanish version (Fonemas de la lengua ignaciana, sec. 1.3), which gives only the primary-stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Stress is phonemic' and 'unpredictable in many words' (p. 58); the 1959 Spanish version supplies the minimal pairs /máyusi/ 'piña' vs /mayúsi/ 'él tiró', /númama/ 'mi piel' vs /numáma/ 'mi mandíbula'. The SPA record also quotes p. 57: after loss of intervocalic glottal stop or /h/ between non-identical vowels 'the second vowel becomes an offglide of the first, which is always stressed' (surface stress shifts from elision).
new_statements.identity_note: Every work is on Ignaciano (Mojeño Ignaciano of San Ignacio de Moxos, Beni, Bolivia; ISO ign), the Otts' own field variety; the Stanford Phonology Archive files it under the heading 'Moxo' with the subheading 'Ignaciano' and cites Ott & Ott 1967 as its sole source, so no other Mojeño variety (Trinitario, Loretano, Javeriano) is involved.

new_statements.relation_note: Placement agrees with the catalog rule string (second syllable; the catalog's own source Ott & Ott 1983 says initial in disyllables, second in longer words 'por lo general'). What it corrects is the 'fixed-strict' (exceptionless) flag: the authors call stress phonemic, give minimal pairs and say it is unpredictable in many words, so the bin is fixed-dominant second-syllable with a lexical initial-stress class (as Carvalho & Rose 2018 p. 21 also state). This is the same correction already recorded in existing_statements 1-2; no new disagreement. New detail relative to the 1959 entry: secondary stress most often penultimate.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic (minimal pairs exist) and not predictable in many words, but the dominant pattern is primary stress on the second syllable of the word; (1967 text adds) secondary stress most often on the penult. I.e. dominant second-syllable stress with a lexical exception class, not an exceptionless rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 1967 p. 58: secondary stress 'most frequently falls on the penult' (not in the 1959 edition). SPA also quotes p. 57: after loss of intervocalic glottal stop or /h/ in unstressed syllables of rapid speech 'the second vowel becomes an offglide of the first, which is always stressed', and p. 56 'Stops tend to be lenis word initial except when in stressed syllables.'
new_statements.exceptions: Stress phonemic with minimal pairs /máyusi/ vs /mayúsi/, /númama/ vs /numáma/ (initial vs second-syllable stress in trisyllables); 'unpredictable in many words'.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Mojeño Ignaciano of San Ignacio de Moxos (Beni, Bolivia), data collected Oct 1956-Oct 1957 'en la vecindad de San Ignacio' by Willis and Rebecca Ott (SIL); not Trinitario.

readall_conflicts: 58, via the Stanford Phonology Archive quotation) says primary stress 'most frequently falls on the second syllable', exactly as the 1959 Spanish version already on record ('recae en la segunda sílaba') and as Carvalho & Rose 2018 (held; 'second underlying syllable', initial in disyllables and some rare trisyllabic nouns). The standing disagreement is one of type, not placement: the Otts call stress phonemic and 'unpredictable in many words', whereas the catalog (StressTyp2) codes Ignaciano as strictly fixed on the second syllable (initial in disyllables). This is the same tension already recorded in existing_statements, and Carvalho & Rose's underlying-second analysis (with prefix-vowel elision producing surface-initial stress) resolves most of the apparent unpredictability. The 1967 English article adds a secondary stress on the penult that the 1959 pamphlet and the catalog do not mention. The three other works (the 1965/1967 grammar sketches and the 1957 accent manuscript) could not be opened, so they neither confirm nor contradict anything. No new conflict. Everything opened (the 1959 Spanish edition of Ott & Ott's phoneme paper and the verbatim p. 58 sentence of its 1967 English printing via SPA 1979) agrees with the catalog on placement (second syllable dominant; initial in disyllables per the 1983 dictionary note) but not with the catalog's 'fixed-strict' flag: the Otts call stress phonemic, cite minimal pairs (/máyusi/ 'piña' vs /mayúsi/ 'he threw'; /númama/ 'my skin…
